hero.title:
Welcome Home,
Welcome Others
hero.subtitle: A guide to the art and calling of homemaking — grounded in Scripture, shaped by love, expressed through hospitality.
hero.verse: "She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy."

competencies.title: Core Competencies of a Homemaker & Wife
competencies.intro: These are not burdens imposed from outside, but gifts cultivated from within — each one an expression of love, wisdom, and faithful stewardship of the home God entrusts to her care.

items.title: Spiritual Anchor
items.description: She roots her home in prayer, Scripture, and worship. Her fear of the Lord is the foundation on which all other competencies rest (Prov. 31:30).
practices: Leading family in Scripture and worship
Cultivating a home atmosphere of peace and faith

items.title: Household Stewardship
items.description: She watches over the affairs of her household with diligence — managing time, resources, and space with intentionality (Prov. 31:27).

items.title: Nourishment & Culinary Art
items.description: She provides food for her household and guests with skill and generosity — the table is her instrument of love (Prov. 31:15).
practices: Adapting to dietary needs of guests

items.title: Nurturing & Caregiving
items.description: She pours herself into the emotional, physical, and spiritual wellbeing of her husband, children, and household (Titus 2:4–5).
practices: Attentive presence with husband and children
Caring for the sick, elderly, or weak

items.title: Hospitality & Welcome
items.description: Her home is a refuge for family, friends, strangers, and the lonely. She makes people feel seen, safe, and celebrated (1 Pet. 4:9; Heb. 13:2).
practices: Keeping a home prepared to receive guests
Hosting meals, gatherings, and overnight guests
Welcoming the stranger and the marginalized

items.title: Creative Excellence
items.description: She brings beauty, craft, and creativity into the home — from décor to handcraft to aesthetics that reflect dignity and delight (Prov. 31:22).
practices: Cultivating a home that reflects care

items.title: Wise Communication
items.description: She speaks with wisdom and kindness — her tongue builds up rather than tears down (Prov. 31:26; Eph. 4:29).
practices: Speaking words of affirmation and encouragement
Listening with empathy and without judgment
Navigating conflict with grace and truth
Teaching others through her words and example

items.title: Industry & Enterprise
items.description: She is not idle — she works with eager hands, contributing to the prosperity of her household (Prov. 31:17–18, 24).
practices: Managing or contributing to household income

items.title: Community & Friendship
items.description: She is embedded in community — giving generously, supporting other women, and building relational networks of care (Gal. 6:2; Titus 2:3–5).
practices: Investing in friendships and neighborly relationships
Serving and giving to those in need
Being an active member of her church family

items.title: Physical & Emotional Wellness
items.description: She attends to her own strength — she cannot pour from an empty vessel. Sabbath rest is an act of faithfulness (Prov. 31:17).
practices: Seeking help and support when needed

manifesto.title: A Biblical Manifesto for Hospitality
manifesto.intro: Hospitality is not a personality trait or a lifestyle aesthetic. It is a command, a calling, and a participation in the very welcome God extends to us through the gospel.

preamble.title: Preamble: The God Who Welcomes
preamble.body: Before we can understand the call to hospitality, we must understand the God who models it. From the beginning, God prepared a garden-home for humanity — a place of provision, beauty, rest, and communion. When humanity broke fellowship with Him through sin, God did not abandon the project of welcome. He set in motion a plan to bring His exiled children home, culminating in the person of Jesus Christ, who "came to seek and save the lost" (Luke 19:10) and who promises that in His Father's house are "many rooms" prepared for those who love Him (John 14:2). Hospitality, then, is not an invented virtue. It is an imitation of God.

pillars.title: We Believe Hospitality Is a Command, Not a Suggestion

scriptures.verse: "Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality."
"Show hospitality to one another without grumbling."

pillars.body: Scripture does not suggest we be hospitable when it is convenient or comfortable. It commands it — plainly, repeatedly, and alongside other moral imperatives like love, generosity, and truth-telling. The hospitable home is not optional obedience. It is the norm of Christian life.

pillars.title: We Believe the Stranger Is to Be Welcomed, Not Feared

scriptures.verse: "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."
"The stranger who sojourns with you shall be to you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself."

pillars.body: The biblical vision of hospitality extends far beyond the familiar. The Greek word philoxenia — translated "hospitality" — literally means "love of the stranger." Israel was commanded to remember they were once strangers in Egypt (Deut. 10:19). We extend welcome because we were welcomed when we were aliens and outsiders (Eph. 2:12–13).

pillars.title: We Believe the Table Is a Theological Act

scriptures.verse: "When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your relatives or rich neighbors... But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind."

pillars.body: Jesus redefined the guest list. The table is not for social reciprocity — it is for grace. It is a foretaste of the great wedding supper of the Lamb, where people will come from east and west, from north and south (Luke 13:29). Every meal shared in love is a small eschatological sign of that coming feast. The home table is a sanctuary of grace.

pillars.title: We Believe Hospitality Requires Presence, Not Perfection

scriptures.verse: "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion."

pillars.body: The story of Mary and Martha is not a rejection of Martha's service — it is a rebuke of her anxiety. Hospitality is not about performance. It is about presence. The goal is not an impressive table; the goal is that your guest encounters love. A simple meal offered with full attention surpasses a feast offered with distraction and stress.

pillars.title: We Believe Hospitality Ministers to Christ Himself

scriptures.verse: "For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me... as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me."

pillars.body: The most radical truth about Christian hospitality is this: in welcoming others, we welcome Christ. He meets us in the face of the stranger, the widow, the lonely neighbor, the grieving friend. To close the door to them is to close the door to Him. To open the door is to open it to our Lord.

pillars.title: We Believe the Hospitable Woman Reflects the Heart of the Church

scriptures.verse: "She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy... She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet."
"She has been hospitable... She has devoted herself to every good work."

pillars.body: The Proverbs 31 woman is generous, prepared, and forward-thinking in her care for others. The widow Paul commends is remembered for her hospitality. The godly woman does not merely manage a household for herself — she opens it for others. Her home becomes a microcosm of the church: a community of welcome, service, and love.

pillars.title: We Commit to a Household of Open Doors
pillars.body: Therefore, we commit to keeping our home as a place of welcome. We will hold our space, time, food, and comfort loosely — as gifts from God to be shared with others. We will not allow busyness, perfectionism, or fear to become excuses for a closed door. We will pray for eyes to see who needs welcome, hands ready to serve, and a table always prepared to receive.
pillars.charge: We do this not to be seen, not to be repaid, and not to impress — but because we have been welcomed by a God of infinite grace, and we are compelled by love to pass that welcome on.

planner.title: The Hospitality Planner
planner.intro: Answer the six questions — Who, What, How, When, Where, and Why — to build a complete, intentional plan for your next act of hospitality.

who.title: Who will you welcome?
who.description: Identify the person or group you feel called to invite. Choose a category, then describe them more specifically below.

guestName.label: Who specifically? (name, group, or description)
guestName.placeholder: e.g., The new family from church, my neighbor Lisa, college students...

guestNeeds.label: What do you know about their needs or current situation?
guestNeeds.placeholder: e.g., Recently moved to town, going through a difficult season, don't have many local connections...

who.scripture: "Do not forget to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some have shown hospitality to angels without knowing it." — Hebrews 13:2

why.title: Why are you extending this hospitality?
why.description: Clarity of purpose shapes everything — from the tone of the gathering to how you prepare your heart.

options.label: Share the gospel / point to Jesus

whyStatement.label: Write your "why" in one or two sentences
whyStatement.placeholder: e.g., I want Sarah to know she is not alone after her miscarriage, and that our home is a safe place for her grief...

prayerIntent.label: What do you want to pray for this person/gathering?
prayerIntent.placeholder: e.g., That they would feel the love of God through our home, that conversation would open doors to their heart...

why.scripture: "We love because he first loved us." — 1 John 4:19

when.title: When will you extend this welcome?
when.description: Choose a time that is intentional and doable — then guard it as you would any other commitment.

eventDate.label: Target date or timeframe
eventDate.placeholder: e.g., This Saturday, within the next two weeks, the first Sunday of the month...

duration.label: Estimated duration
duration.placeholder: e.g., 2 hours, all afternoon, the whole weekend...

when.scripture: "She gets up while it is still night; she provides food for her family and portions for her female servants." — Proverbs 31:15

where.title: Where will you host?
where.description: The setting shapes the experience. Choose the location that best serves your guests and your purpose.

spaceNotes.label: Any notes on space preparation or accessibility?
spaceNotes.placeholder: e.g., Need to set up the guest room, borrow extra chairs, consider wheelchair access...

where.scripture: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it." — Proverbs 15:17

what.title: What will you offer?
what.description: Think through the practical gifts of food, activity, and provision you will bring to your guests.

menuIdeas.label: Menu ideas or specific dishes
menuIdeas.placeholder: e.g., Pot roast, salad, sourdough bread, apple pie; or simple pasta with salad and garlic bread...

specialNeeds.label: Any dietary restrictions or special needs to accommodate?
specialNeeds.placeholder: e.g., Gluten-free, nut allergy, vegetarian, young children present...

what.scripture: "She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness." — Proverbs 31:27

how.title: How will you prepare — practically and spiritually?
how.description: Great hospitality flows from preparation of both the home and the heart.

options.label: Send invitation or personally reach out
Plan and shop for the menu
Clean and prepare the home space
Arrange childcare or include children in plans
Pray specifically for each guest by name
Ask God for love, patience, and presence
Re-read your "why" statement before they arrive
Commit to being fully present, not distracted
Choose to serve joyfully, without resentment

helpNeeded.label: Who can help you prepare? (delegate something)
helpNeeded.placeholder: e.g., Husband picks up groceries, kids set the table, friend brings dessert...

extraNotes.label: Any other notes or intentions for this gathering
extraNotes.placeholder: e.g., I want to make sure to ask Sarah about her job search. I want to end the evening with prayer together...

how.scripture: "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters." — Colossians 3:23

plan.title: Your Plan Is Ready
plan.description: Here is your complete hospitality plan. Print it, save it, or simply carry it in your heart.
plan.closingVerse: "When you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you."

schaeffer.title: The Hidden Art of Homemaking
schaeffer.intro: Few voices in the twentieth century spoke with more theological depth and practical beauty about homemaking than Edith Schaeffer — missionary, author, artist, hostess, and co-founder of L'Abri Fellowship. Her work gives the calling of homemaker a richly grounded, beautifully articulated vision that still speaks today.
schaeffer.bio: Born in China in 1914 to missionary parents (her Chinese name, Mei Fuh, means "beautiful happiness"), Edith married Francis Schaeffer in 1935. Together they co-founded L'Abri Fellowship in Switzerland in 1955 — a community of radical hospitality where seekers, skeptics, and the spiritually wounded could come with honest questions. She authored or co-authored more than 20 books and was listed among 100 Christian Women Who Changed the Twentieth Century. Her signature work, The Hidden Art of Homemaking (1971), remains the most theologically rich treatment of domestic creativity in evangelical literature.

themes.title: The First Artist: Imago Dei as Foundation
themes.body: Schaeffer's entire vision of homemaking rests on one premise: because God is the first and supreme Artist — who made a world of beauty, variety, and design — human beings made in His image carry a creative impulse that must be expressed, not suppressed. Creativity in the home is not a luxury. It is an expression of bearing the divine image.
themes.quote: If you have been afraid that your love of beautiful flowers and the flickering flame of the candle is somehow less spiritual than living in starkness and ugliness, remember that He who created you to be creative gave you the things with which to make beauty.

themes.title: The Hidden Art: Domestic Life as Artistic Expression
themes.body: "Hidden" is deliberate: these are arts hidden in plain sight, embedded in cooking, decorating, gardening, flower arranging, writing letters, setting a table. She argued that every person has an unfulfilled creative talent waiting to be expressed in their own sphere — and that the home is the most immediate canvas available.
themes.quote: I would define 'hidden art' as the art found in the ordinary areas of everyday life. Each person has, I believe, some talent which is unfulfilled in some hidden area of his being — a talent which could be expressed and developed.

themes.title: No Sacred/Secular Divide: All of Life Before God
themes.body: Rooted in the Reformed conviction that all of life is lived coram Deo — before the face of God — Schaeffer insisted there is no divide between the spiritual life and what she did as a wife and mother. Cooking a meal, sewing curtains, setting a welcoming table — all could be acts of worship as genuine as any prayer.
themes.quote: There is no occasion when meals should become totally unimportant. Meals can be very small indeed, very inexpensive — but they should always be more than just food.

themes.title: The Apologetics of Beauty: Hospitality as Witness
themes.body: Schaeffer argued that beauty itself functions apologetically. A warm home, a beautiful table, a fragrant meal do not merely comfort the body — they make Christianity plausible and desirable to the searching soul. Nancy Pearcey, who encountered L'Abri as a young agnostic, described "an apologetics of beauty that made me want Christianity to be true."
themes.quote: We are as concerned for living as we are for thinking. From the beginning, the concern has been that the truth is as much exhibited in everyday life as it is defended in discussion.

themes.title: What Is a Family? — The Home as Many Things at Once
themes.body: In her 1975 book, Schaeffer defines the family through a series of rich metaphors: a museum of memories, a perpetual relay of truth, a shelter in time of storm, a door with hinges and a lock, an ever-changing mobile, a formation center for human relationships, and a birthplace of creativity. Each metaphor unlocks a different dimension of what the home is called to be.
themes.quote: There needs to be a homemaker exercising some measure of skill, imagination, creativity, desire to fulfill needs and give pleasure to others in the family. How precious a thing is the human family. Is it not worth some sacrifice in time, energy, safety, discomfort, work?

schaeffer.labriTitle: L'Abri: A Living Model of Hospitality
schaeffer.labriBody: In 1955, the Schaeffers opened their chalet in Huémoz, Switzerland, to anyone who came with honest questions. L'Abri — French for "the shelter" — began with afternoon teas for neighborhood girls and grew, by 1960, into a community so remarkable that Time magazine took notice. Edith's Sunday evening High Tea hosted upwards of 50 visitors from around the world each week. She ran it on faith-based finances with no missions budget, sometimes managing unannounced busloads of young people — and as those who were there remember, "inexpensive and homemade did not mean ugly."
labriPrinciples: No formal fundraising — the community ran entirely on prayer
Guests welcomed for an afternoon or up to three months
Daily life integrated: study, shared chores, communal meals
Beauty cultivated on a missionary budget — candles, linens, cut flowers
Biblical grounding: Matthew 25:31–40 — welcoming the stranger as welcoming Christ
schaeffer.labriQuote: "I have never met anyone with such a passion for God, combined with a passion for people, combined with a passion for truth."

pullQuotes.quote: If you have two loaves of bread, sell one and buy a lily. The bread becomes a different thing when eaten at a table with the lily in the center.
Your home is not something for a misty future — TODAY is your life.
It is not a waste to write beautiful prose or poetry for one person's eyes alone.
People throw away what they could have by insisting on perfection, which they cannot have, and looking for it where they will never find it.

books.title: The Hidden Art of Homemaking
books.desc: Her masterwork. Fourteen chapters on creativity in domestic life — music, cooking, decorating, gardening, writing — all grounded in the theology of Imago Dei.

books.title: What Is a Family?
books.desc: Defines the family through eight creative metaphors. Covers the full arc of family life without flinching at hardship, aging, or loss.

books.title: L'Abri
books.desc: The first-person account of how L'Abri began — part memoir, part theology of hospitality, entirely compelling.

footer.verse: "She is clothed with strength and dignity; she can laugh at the days to come. She speaks with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue."
footer.tagline: The Gracious Home — A tool for the faithful homemaker
